posts.title: The Time Never Made It to My Pocket
posts.body:
It’s 9pm on a weekend and I’m in bed with my laptop, building a portfolio nobody asked me to build.
Work ended hours ago. This is the other job. The unpaid one, where I put together proof that I’m the kind of product manager who’s fast now, and still worth hiring in a market that changed its mind about what that means.
I could tell you I’m exhausted. It’d be half true.
But that’s not really why I’m here. A product manager who doesn’t understand her own product is useless. My product is turning into an AI product. So I’m turning myself into someone who understands AI products, on my own evenings, before anyone makes me. That’s not panic. That’s the job.
Here’s the part that gets me.
AI was supposed to give me time, and it does. A ticket for a serious feature used to eat a couple of hours. I write it in thirty minutes now, and it comes out sharper than what I’d have written by hand.
The time is real. I just can’t find where it went.
Because the moment a two-hour task takes thirty minutes, the difference doesn’t come back to me as ninety minutes of my life. It becomes the new expectation. “Great, you’re faster. Start on y.”
In 1930, Keynes told his readers their grandchildren would work fifteen-hour weeks. The machines would handle the rest. He had the machines right. He had the productivity right.
He just assumed we’d keep the time.
“With AI, productivity should triple”
Someone will say this in a meeting you’re in. Maybe they already have.
It sounds like a compliment to the tools. It isn’t. It’s a number, and the number is now yours.
Watch what the sentence does. It takes the ceiling of what AI made possible on your single best day and quietly installs it as the floor you’re measured against every day. The thing you pulled off once, caffeinated and a little lucky, is now just Tuesday.
And the strange thing is, I don’t even hate the work. That’s what makes this hard to write.
I like this stuff. Genuinely. Some of those evenings in bed with the laptop are the most interesting hours of my week. Watching a model do something I couldn’t have done at all a year ago still gives me a small jolt I haven’t gotten tired of. If the only story here were exhaustion, I’d have…

posts.title: AI didn't kill your hard skills, it killed your evidence.
posts.body:
Everyone keeps telling you the same thing this year. Stop worrying about the technical stuff. Lean into your soft skills, the human part, the thing no machine can copy. It’s the safe advice of 2026.
I think it’s backwards.
Here’s what nobody says out loud: your soft skills were never the safe part. They were just the part nobody could ever see.
Think about what your hard skills actually gave you. Not just the ability, but the receipt. The engineer had the code. The designer had the mockup. The analyst had the model. The PM had the spec. Whatever your job, you had an artifact that did your arguing for you, something you could point to that said, without you having to say it, I can do the thing.
Then AI made those artifacts producible by anyone. The proof collapsed across the board.
Picture yourself updating your CV, the cursor just blinking. The technical bullets are still there, the tools, the stack, the things you spent years learning to do. But you already know how they read now. Anyone can build things. The barrier you cleared is a weekend and a subscription for the person applying next to you.
So you try to write down what actually made you good. That you knew what to build and what to kill. That you held the room together when the deadline slipped. That you could read which no in the meeting was the real one.
And you delete it before you finish the line. Has judgment. Good with people. Knows what matters. It sounds like exactly what someone with none of it would write.
That’s the trap. And every important person is telling you it’s good news. Jamie Dimon says build your EQ and you’ll have plenty of jobs. Satya Nadella says IQ still has its place, but it’s no longer the only thing the world needs.
They’re right that the human skills matter. They’re wrong about what just happened to you.
Your soft skills were never the safe part
Because your judgment never left a receipt in the first place. Your taste. Your knack for killing the wrong project before it burns a quarter. Where’s the artifact? What’s the commit?
There isn’t one. There never was. Good judgment looks exactly like luck from the outside, a decision that happened to work. You can’t screenshot it.
